scarcity: Resources are limited relative to the wants people seek to satisfy.
opportunity cost: The value of the next-best alternative forgone when a choice is made.
capital: Produced resources used to make other goods and services; financial capital must be distinguished when that sense is intended.
labour: Human physical and mental effort used in production.
entrepreneurship: Organising productive resources and bearing the risk of business decisions.
specialisation: Concentrating productive activity on a narrower range of tasks or products.
division of labour: Splitting a production process into tasks performed by different workers or groups.
market economy: An economy in which market prices and private decisions play the main role in allocating resources.
planned economy: An economy in which government planning directs the main resource-allocation decisions.
mixed economy: An economy combining market allocation with government ownership, provision or intervention.
private sector: Economic activity owned and controlled by private individuals or organisations.
public sector: Economic activity owned or controlled by government.
sole proprietor: An individual who owns an unincorporated business and bears its business obligations personally.
partnership: A business owned jointly by partners; avoid unsupported universal legal membership limits.
private company: An incorporated business whose shares are not offered freely to the general public.
public company: A company permitted to offer shares to the public; this does not mean government ownership.
multinational company: A business with productive operations in more than one country; this describes geographic operations rather than a universal legal form.
co-operative: An organisation owned by members to pursue their common economic interests.
close corporation: An incorporated business with member ownership; describe the syllabus-level distinction without inventing current statutory thresholds.
public corporation: An organisation established for public purposes and owned or controlled by the state.
trade union: An organisation representing workers in dealings with employers.
employers' association: An organisation representing the interests of employers, often within an industry.
collective bargaining: Negotiation between representatives of workers and employers over matters such as pay and working conditions.
money: An asset generally accepted as a means of payment and used to express value.
homogeneity of money: Uniformity of units of the same denomination, rather than equality of value across different denominations.
central bank: An institution responsible for currency, monetary arrangements and banking-system functions such as acting as banker to government and banks.
commercial bank: A bank providing deposit, payment and lending services to customers.
stock exchange: An organised market for trading shares and other financial securities.
exchange rate: The value of one currency expressed in terms of another currency.
depreciation: A fall in a currency's value relative to other currencies under market determination.
appreciation: A rise in a currency's value relative to other currencies under market determination.
market: An arrangement through which buyers and sellers interact to exchange a product and determine its price.
demand: The quantities buyers are willing and able to buy at different prices over a stated period, other relevant conditions unchanged.
supply: The quantities producers are willing and able to offer at different prices over a stated period, other relevant conditions unchanged.
equilibrium: A price and quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
price elasticity of demand: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a price change, measured by percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price.
price elasticity of supply: The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a price change, measured by percentage change in quantity supplied divided by percentage change in price.
joint demand: Demand for goods used together, such as complementary products.
substitute: A good that can serve as an alternative to another good in meeting a similar want.
perfect competition: A market model with many small price-taking firms selling homogeneous products, with entry and exit and relevant information available.
monopoly: A market with a single seller of the relevant product; define the relevant market before making the claim.
disposable income: Income available for spending and saving after relevant taxes and deductions.
real income: Income adjusted for the price level, indicating purchasing power.
economic rent: The part of a factor's reward above the minimum needed to keep it in its current use.
transfer earnings: The minimum reward needed to retain a factor in its current use.
production: The creation of goods and services or addition of value through productive activity.
productivity: Output per unit of input over a specified period.
total cost: The sum of fixed and variable costs at a specified output.
fixed cost: A cost that does not vary with output over the relevant period and capacity range; its level can change over time.
variable cost: A cost that varies with the level of output over the relevant period.
total revenue: The amount received from sales; for a single product at one price, price multiplied by quantity sold.
average revenue: Total revenue divided by quantity sold.
marginal revenue: The additional revenue from selling one more unit.
marginal cost: The additional cost of producing one more unit.
profit: Total revenue minus total cost over the stated period.
profit maximisation: Choosing the feasible output or decision giving the highest profit; the relevant marginal-cost/marginal-revenue condition needs the appropriate maximising context.
economies of scale: Reductions in long-run average cost as the scale of production increases.
diseconomies of scale: Increases in long-run average cost as the scale of production increases.
fiscal policy: Use of government spending and taxation to pursue economic objectives.
monetary policy: Use of monetary and credit conditions, including interest rates and money supply, to pursue economic objectives.
budget deficit: Government expenditure exceeds government revenue over the stated period.
budget surplus: Government revenue exceeds government expenditure over the stated period.
proportional tax: A tax whose rate remains a constant proportion of the relevant income or tax base.
progressive tax: A tax for which the proportion of income paid in tax rises as income rises.
regressive tax: A tax for which the proportion of income paid in tax falls as income rises.
inflation: A sustained increase in the general price level, reducing the purchasing power of money.
retail price index: An index tracking changes in the cost of a weighted basket of consumer goods and services relative to a base period.
unemployment: People of working age who are willing and able to work and seeking work but unable to find it, subject to the stated measurement convention.
Gross Domestic Product: The value of final goods and services produced within an economy over a stated period.
Gross National Product: Domestic product adjusted for net primary income from abroad in the syllabus's national-product terminology.
National Income: Income generated by the factors of production of an economy over a stated period; state the measurement basis when comparing totals.
economic growth: An increase in real output over time; distinguish total growth from growth per person.
balance of trade: The value of goods exports minus the value of goods imports over a stated period.
balance of payments: A record of economic transactions between residents of an economy and the rest of the world over a stated period.
absolute advantage: Ability to produce more output with the same resources, or the same output with fewer resources.
comparative advantage: Ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.
net migration: Immigration minus emigration over a stated period; a rate additionally requires a stated population denominator.
natural population change: Births minus deaths over a stated period, excluding migration.
life expectancy: The average number of years a person is expected to live under the stated mortality conditions.
external cost: An uncompensated cost of an activity borne by a third party.
public good: A good whose consumption is non-rival and non-excludable in the relevant setting.
merit good: A good judged beneficial to users and society that may be underconsumed when decisions are left entirely to the market.
free good: A good available without sacrificing scarce resources at the relevant margin; a zero monetary price does not establish this.
investment: In the productive sense, expenditure adding to capital goods; distinguish financial purchases or deposits when the context uses that sense.
quota: A physical or quantity limit on the specified imports, production or extraction.
subsidy: Government financial assistance that supports an activity, such as reducing producers' costs.
opportunity-cost comparison: Comparison of the valued alternatives forgone by different feasible decisions, using a consistent time horizon and relevant constraints.
